transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-04-04
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Alex Morgan, Samir Patel (Redwood); Dana Liu, Miguel Torres, Priya Sethi (Veridian)

Summary (auto-gen, may be rough):
Quick POC scoping focused on latency and throughput SLOs for Veridian Health: discussed TTFT vs TPOT, target p95/p99 numbers, measurement approach (synthetic vs production traces), and steps to run benchmarks. Action items and next steps agreed.

Topics:
- Success criteria (latency SLOs, throughput)
- Workload sizing and example traces
- Measurement plan and tools (harness, warm vs cold, batching, KV cache)
- Timeline and responsibilities

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: hey everyone, thanks for carving out time, i'll kick off — alex from redwood, our se samir's here.  
[00:07] Samir: hi all.
[00:09] Dana: thanks, alex, we appreciate it. we want to make sure the POC proves we can hit sub-100ms tail latencies for interactive flows and also sustain X rps for background batch tasks.
[00:18] Alex: great, that's exactly what we wanted to scope. just to align terminology, when we say TTFT we mean time to first token, and TPOT is time per output token, right?
[00:25] Miguel: yeah, that's correct — for our UI latency we care about TTFT and p95/p99 specifically. for throughput we also want tp90 of tokens per second on the backend.
[00:34] Samir: quick clarification, when you say sub-100ms tail, do you mean p95 or p99? those are very different—
[00:40] Dana: p99 ideally, but if p95 is 80-90ms and p99 is 150ms that might be acceptable. our threshold for user-facing is p99 < 200ms.
[00:48] Alex: okay so target: TTFT p95 = 80-100ms, TTFT p99 = <200ms as a stretch. TPOT targets for streaming: p95 token latency ~20-30ms and p99 <60ms? is that in line with expectations?
[00:58] Priya: that seems reasonable, but depends a lot on prompt length and model choice — small-ish model vs 70B changes numbers drastically. our workload average output length is ~40 tokens, median 20.
[01:10] Samir: correct, model selection matters. for the POC we recommend we test 3 configs: hosted managed model (lower commit, variable), dedicated GPU pool with bfloat quant, and a quantized on-prem variant if you want private. we'll instrument TTFT and TPOT separately.
[01:22] Miguel: for sizing, our peak concurrency estimate is 120 concurrent interactive users, apdex-ish load, and background jobs are about 2k TPS burst for embeddings — but for generation it's more like 600 tokens per second sustained across a dedicated pool.
[01:34] Alex: ok that gives us numbers to design the load. typical POC benchmarks we'll run: synthetic replay from your traces, plus synthetic spike tests (50%-200% peak) to validate fallbacks.
[01:44] Dana: we can share traces, but heads up, traces have PII redacted, may be a little messy.
[01:49] Priya: yes we'll provide 7 days of traffic, sample traces and 1k representative prompts.
[01:54] Samir: cool. on measurement plan — we'll measure:
- cold TTFT (first request to idle runtime)
- warm TTFT (after model loaded and KV cache primed)
- TPOT across token positions (early tokens vs later tokens)
- tail percentiles p50/p95/p99 and histograms

[02:12] Alex: and we'll also report CPU/GPU utilization, batch sizes, and queue times so you can tune batching vs latency tradeoffs.
[02:18] Miguel: what about KV cache effects — our chat flows are very prefix-heavy, cache reuse should help a lot. we need to see both cold and steady-state with cache warm.
[02:26] Samir: yes, we'll run warm-cached traces as a primary SLO measurement. measurement approach: run production-like replay for 30 minutes steady-state, capture percentiles, then run 10x spike test for resilience.
[02:36] Dana: tools: do we use wrk or does redwood provide a harness? we prefer to run things in our env if possible.
[02:41] Samir: we can provide our benchmark harness (python/locust based) and artifacts. for on-prem we'll give dockerized runner; for hosted/dedicated we can run the harness from our infra against your test endpoint — whichever you prefer.
[02:51] Alex: also note that TTFT has components: network hop + load balancer + cold boot + model first token generation. we'll separate network overhead by running internal-to-internal tests where possible.
[03:01] Priya: how do you simulate user think time and interactive jitter? that's big for UI latency.
[03:05] Samir: harness supports poisson arrivals and configurable think time, so we can model that. we'll include a UI-tailored scenario and a backend burst scenario.
[03:12] Miguel: on metrics, we need exported traces and percentiles in a csv plus rug plots. also we need reproducible scripts so we can rerun after changes.
[03:20] Alex: we'll deliver raw telemetry, per-request logs (anonymized), and a summary with p50/p95/p99 and recommended tuning knobs.
[03:27] Dana: can you show differences between quantization levels? we have concerns about quality regression.
[03:31] Samir: yes, part of POC we'll include a quality check: run 200 sample prompts across configs and compute Rouge/embedding-similarity/heuristic checks. we'll correlate latency improvements with quality drop.
[03:41] Priya: for SLOs, we want explicit acceptance criteria: e.g., TTFT p95 <= 100ms AND quality drop <= 2% embedding-sim. this becomes pass/fail for a given config.
[03:52] Alex: agreed, we'll draft success criteria with thresholds per config.
[03:56] Miguel: timeline? we want POC to finish in 3 weeks, with first benchmarks in week 1 and tuning in week 2.
[04:02] Alex: realistic timeline: day 0-2 onboarding and sample data exchange, day 3-7 run initial baseline benchmarks, day 8-12 optimize configs + run more benchmarks, day 13-21 validation and final report. seems doable.
[04:14] Dana: risks: SSO and data access delays, and onboard time for on-prem hardware if we go that route.
[04:19] Samir: noted — if on-prem we need extra 1-2 weeks for network and HSM/KMS setup for keys.
[04:25] Alex: logistics: we'll need a test API key for hosted, and if you want dedicated we'll provision a small reserved pool for the POC. also we'll need a contact for infra (miguel) and ml (priya).
[04:35] Miguel: will do.
[04:36] Alex: (brief) competitors — you mentioned cloudx and anthro earlier; we'll include a comparison table in the plan.
[04:42] Dana: yes that would be helpful.
[04:44] Alex: ok recap of action items and owners: alex sends POC plan + pricing, samir shares harness and scripts, priya provides traces and prompts, dana confirms access and SSO. target deliverables by next week, first runs by April 6.
[04:58] Priya: sounds good, one more question — how do you handle burst fallback if dedicated pool is saturated?
[05:03] Samir: we have routing policies that can failover to a lower-cost or hosted model with graceful degradation; we'll show expected latency curves in the report.
[05:12] Dana: perfect, thanks.
[05:14] Alex: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the plan and calendar invite for the kickoff bench run.
[05:20] Miguel: thanks.

End of transcript.

POC measurement plan (short bullets auto-summary):
- Success criteria: TTFT p95 <= 100ms (primary), TTFT p99 < 200ms (stretch), TPOT p95 ~20-30ms, quality drop <= 2% embedding-similarity for quantized configs.
- Workload sizing: 120 concurrent interactive users, avg output 40 tokens, background generation ~600 TPS sustained.
- Benchmarks: 30-min steady-state replay (warm cache), cold-start TTFT tests, 10x spike resilience test, quality-run of 200 prompts.
- Tools: Redwood harness (locust/wrk hybrid), option to run in-customer replay; capture per-request logs and histograms.
- Metrics: p50/p95/p99 TTFT and TPOT, batch sizes, GPU util, queue time, model and kernel config.
- Timeline: sample data + keys (day 0-2), baseline runs (day 3-7), tuning and re-runs (day 8-12), validation + report (day 13-21).
